lesson.title: Half Old, Half New: The Semiconservative Model of Replication
lesson.summary: Each new DNA double helix produced by replication is made of one original parental strand and one newly synthesized strand, a model of replication confirmed experimentally by Meselson and Stahl in 1958.
lesson.body:
Once scientists understood that DNA replication used each strand of the double helix as a template (as described in the DNA Replication chapter), a question remained: how exactly do the old and new strands end up arranged in the two resulting double helices? Researchers in the 1950s proposed three competing possibilities. In the conservative model, the original double helix would stay completely intact, and an entirely new double helix made of two new strands would be built alongside it. In the semiconservative model, each of the two resulting helices would contain one original strand and one newly made strand. In the dispersive model, both resulting helices would be patchworks of old and new DNA scattered along their length.

Matthew Meselson and Franklin Stahl settled the question with a now classic experiment. They grew E. coli bacteria for many generations in a medium containing a heavy isotope of nitrogen, 15N, so that all the bacteria's DNA became labeled as heavy. They then switched the bacteria to normal medium containing the common, lighter isotope, 14N, and let them replicate. Using density gradient centrifugation, a technique that separates molecules by weight, they tracked how the density of the DNA changed over successive rounds of replication. After one round of replication in the light medium, all of the DNA appeared at a single density exactly intermediate between fully heavy and fully light DNA. This result alone ruled out the conservative model, which would have predicted two separate bands, one still fully heavy and one fully light. After a second round of replication, two bands appeared: one at the intermediate density and one at the fully light density, in roughly equal amounts. This pattern ruled out the dispersive model, which would have predicted the DNA simply growing lighter and lighter as a single band, and it matched exactly what the semiconservative model predicted.

This experiment is why DNA polymerase works the way it does: rather than building a wholly new double helix somewhere else, it moves along each original strand of the opened double helix and builds a new complementary partner directly beside it, so every daughter helix ends up with one old strand and one new one. The semiconservative model also explains why replication is so reliable across generations of cells: each new helix retains one strand of the original, undamaged genetic sequence, which helps preserve genetic information faithfully from one generation of cells to the next, and gives repair systems (covered later in this unit) an intact template strand to work from when errors need to be corrected.
